summary:
Qatar criminalises consensual same-sex relations under Article 296 of the Penal Code (Law 11/2004), which carries one to three years' imprisonment. The provision applies to Muslims and non-Muslims alike and covers sexual acts between men and between women. For Muslims convicted in sharia courts a capital sentence remains a theoretical possibility; it has never been imposed. No statute repealing or legalising this exposure appears in the sources. Article 296 replaced Article 201 of the 1971 Penal Code, which had carried up to five years, and before that Article 171 of the 1956 code and the Indian Penal Code imposed through Order in Council in 1938.

Trans people face a separate detention power. They may be held for up to six months without trial or charge on suspicion of "impersonating the opposite gender" or of violating "public morality" and "community protection" provisions.

Qatar does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and cohabitation is itself illegal. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex has no route to formal recognition, and shared accommodation with a partner carries its own exposure.

Enforcement reaches visitors. Human Rights Watch documented six cases of severe repeated beatings and five cases of sexual harassment in police custody between 2019 and 2022, with arrests in public places made solely on the basis of gender expression and searches conducted unlawfully; mistreatment continued as recently as September 2022, as Qatar prepared to host the World Cup.

On 4 February 2024 a dual British-Mexican citizen was arrested after police ran a fake Grindr profile. He was held for 44 days, interrogated about other gay men, forced to sign documents in Arabic without a translator and denied a lawyer. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention raised concerns about his treatment. Detainees in that case were also denied access to antiretroviral medicines needed to live with HIV, a denial the Working Group flagged.

In May 2023 Gilbert Ignatius, a Qatar Airways employee, was detained by the Criminal Investigation Department over his appearance, with tinted moisturizer, designer clothing and a bag cited as evidence of prostitution. An officer told him "You have no rights. This is Qatar," and struck him when he asked to contact the Indonesian embassy. He was later deported, fired and banned from Qatar without official explanation. Ignatius reported that post-World Cup secret police operations especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand.

Earlier cases include the Polish Instagram figure King Luxy, held for two months in 2016 on suspicion of being homosexual, and an American visitor sentenced in 1998 to six months in prison and 90 lashes for homosexual activity. In the 1990s the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration told Philippine workers that gay workers were prohibited in Qatar, following mass arrests and deportations.

Abuse in custody has included beatings, torture and forced "conversion therapy". A May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed, the first Qatari to come out publicly as gay, described LGBTQ people being held and physically abused, then promised safety from further torture if they agreed to inform on others. Trans detainees are required to undergo forced physical detransition, including surgical removal of breast tissue, while held, and must attend conversion "therapy" on release, according to BBC-sourced information that Qatari authorities "categorically rejected".

Public expression is policed. Nasser Al Khater said in December 2021 that public display of affection "is frowned upon", and Major General al-Ansari warned that rainbow flags could be confiscated to "protect" fans. In May 2022 the Emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, said LGBTQ visitors would be welcomed to the World Cup but must respect the nation's culture; the 2013 bid chief Hassan Al-Thawadi had said all were welcome provided they refrained from public displays of affection. Some hotels on FIFA's official recommended accommodation list refused to serve same-sex couples outright in May 2022, while others accepted them only if they hid the relationship in public; FIFA said it would remind hotels of non-discrimination requirements.

Campaigning for LGBTQ rights is not permitted. In 2022 police arrested protesters who criticised Qatari law.

In 2013 Kuwait proposed banning gay foreigners from entering any Gulf Cooperation Council country. The GCC agreed to discuss the proposal and then backtracked, possibly over concerns about the effect on Qatar's 2022 World Cup hosting.
tangentialFactors:
Qatar voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity at the Human Rights Council in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025.

In 2018 nine articles on gay and transgender rights were censored from the Doha edition of The New York Times International Edition, and the Government Communications Office pledged an investigation. In June 2019 the state-linked outlet AJ+ marked LGBTQ Pride Month, drawing criticism over the contrast with domestic censorship. A 2016 opinion piece in Doha News by a gay Qatari man writing under a pseudonym drew extremely strong reactions for allowing the topic to be discussed at all.

The Australian men's national football team publicly called in October 2022 for Qatar to recognise same-sex marriage.

In 2022 Transport for London banned Qatari advertising after Qatar moved to block rainbow armbands at the World Cup; Qatar subsequently reviewed its London investments.
localsOnly:
Residents who are detained face release conditions that visitors generally do not: trans detainees must attend conversion "therapy" after release, and detainees have been pressed to become informants against other LGBTQ people in exchange for safety from further torture.

Cohabitation is illegal, which affects unmarried residents sharing a home as well as long-stay visitors.

Qatar Airways employee Gilbert Ignatius was fired and banned from Qatar after his May 2023 detention, without official explanation. Migrant workers who appear to be LGBTQ are reported to be especially targeted in post-World Cup police operations.

The government does not allow people in Qatar to campaign for LGBTQ rights, and police arrested protesters who criticised Qatari law in 2022.
outOfScopeNotes:
The capital sentence for same-gender sex has never been imposed, and one line of argument holds that because same-gender couples cannot marry, the penalty applies only to Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions. The sources do not resolve how that reading would operate in practice.

The account of forced surgical detransition of trans detainees is attributed to BBC-sourced information; Qatari authorities "categorically rejected" it. No independent confirmation appears in the inventory.

The Government Communications Office pledged an investigation into the 2018 censorship of articles on gay and transgender rights from the Doha edition of The New York Times International Edition; the outcome is not sourced.

Whether the 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council proposal to ban gay foreigners from entry was abandoned permanently, or only shelved, is not established by the sources.
